description:
I'm Mola, a UI/UX Designer planning to build a simple, interactive virtual space exploration app for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. I'm interested in creating an engaging experience that allows users to explore forgotten space artifacts through interactive discoveries and storytelling.

I plan to work independently on this project, but if you're interested in joining me, feel free to reach out at molami137@gmail.com.
summary: Space Relics is an interactive virtual museum that brings the stories of NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars to life. Through an immersive journey across space, visitors can discover historic spacecraft, rovers, and scientific instruments, learning about their missions, discoveries, contributions to space exploration, and a fun fact. It was designed for learners of all ages. Space Relics combines visual storytelling, interactive exploration, and multilingual accessibility to transform forgotten space hardware into engaging educational experiences.
details:
The Idea

When most people think about space exploration, it is often just the astronauts, discoveries, and successful missions. However, the machines that made many of these achievements possible are sometimes overlooked, especially when they are no longer in action.

I created Space Relics to tell the stories of these machines and introduce learners of all ages to their contributions to space exploration.

Space Relics is an interactive virtual museum that takes visitors on a mission from Earth to the Moon and then Mars, where they can discover six pieces of NASA equipment and learn about their history, purpose, and scientific achievements.

How It Works

The experience begins just outside Earth, on a space deck, where visitors are introduced to their mission. After selecting Begin Mission, they travel through space to the Moon.

Upon arrival, visitors explore a lunar environment containing three discovery markers. Selecting a marker activates a scanning animation that reveals a piece of NASA equipment.

Each discovery includes:

  • An image of the equipment.
  • Its name and mission details.
  • Its location and operational status.
  • The story behind its mission.
  • Its contributions to space exploration.
  • An interesting fun fact.

After discovering the three lunar relics, visitors continue their journey to Mars, where they investigate three additional pieces of equipment using the same interactive discovery system.

Once all six relics have been discovered, visitors return to Earth and receive a mission completion summary showing all their discoveries and the worlds explored.

Featured NASA Equipment

The virtual museum currently features six pieces of equipment:

Moon

  • Surveyor 3
  • Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
  • Apollo 14 Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP)

Mars

  • Opportunity Rover
  • InSight Lander
  • Ingenuity Helicopter

Creativity and Storytelling

Rather than presenting the NASA equipment as a collection of photographs with descriptions, Space Relics turns it into an interactive space mission.

Visitors become explorers who travel between worlds, investigate discovery markers, scan objects, and gradually uncover their stories through a simulated space exploration experience.

The experience follows three principles: Explore, Discover, Learn.

Accessibility and Educational Impact

Space Relics was designed for learners of different ages and backgrounds. To make it accessible to a wider audience, the website offers eight language options: English, Spanish, French, Arabic, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, and Portuguese.

The project aims to make space history easier to understand, encourage curiosity about STEM subjects, and demonstrate that equipment left behind after a mission is an important part of the story of our journey to infinity.

It could serve as a supplementary learning resource for schools, science clubs, and educational programmes, especially after the relics database has been expanded.

Tools and Technologies

Space Relics was developed as a responsive web application using:

  • Figma: For UI/UX design and interface planning.
  • React: For building the interactive user interface and reusable components.
  • JavaScript: For implementing navigation, discovery interactions, animations, and mission progression.
  • HTML and CSS: For page structure, styling, responsive layouts, and visual effects.
  • Vite: For frontend development and production builds.
  • i18next: For implementing multilingual support.
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): Used for AI-assisted code generation, debugging, troubleshooting, educational content support, translation assistance, and generation of the spaceship artwork featured in the space-travel animation. The project concept, UI/UX designs, and creative direction were developed by me.
  • Git and GitHub: For version control and hosting the project's source code.
  • Vercel: For deploying the website and making it publicly accessible.

NASA mission information and imagery were used to support the educational content and equipment stories, with relevant image credits and links included in the experience.

Design Considerations and Future Development

Space Relics was developed as a solo-team project with AI-assisted coding.

As the sole team member, I came up with the project, researched the NASA equipment, designed the user experience and interfaces, directed the implementation, tested the website, identified issues, requested corrections, and managed the final deployment.

ChatGPT generated the application code based on my design specifications and instructions. Through an iterative process, I reviewed the results, provided feedback, requested modifications, and tested the updated implementation until the experience matched my intended design and functionality.

During development, I focused on creating an engaging experience that could run in a regular web browser without requiring specialised equipment or software.

I also considered responsive design, straightforward navigation, readability, image optimisation, and multilingual accessibility.

Space Relics currently features six NASA relics across two worlds, but the concept could be expanded to include more equipment, missions, interactive learning activities, and educational resources.

Conclusion

Space Relics is built around one idea: The left-behind equipment is not just space junk.
